C001035.text: Today, the Senate HELP Committee voted to advance bipartisan legislation I introduced with Senators Tim Kaine and Lisa Murkowski to prevent the Department of Education from transferring critical offices responsible for special education and rehabilitative services, postsecondary education, elementary and secondary education, and Indian education to other federal agencies that lack the staff and expertise needed to execute their missions. One of the offices protected by our bill manages programs established under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, known as IDEA, that help meet the educational needs of more than 8 million children with disabilities. Moving this work to the Department of Health and Human Services fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of the Special Education program. It is focused primarily on students’ educational needs, not their health care needs. Every American, regardless of background or disability, deserves access to a quality public education. B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

Community health centers play a critical role in ensuring families have access to primary care, preventive services, and essential healthcare close to home, especially in rural communities. I’ll continue working to secure federal resources that strengthen healthcare access and support healthier communities across our region.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

I have heard the same message from Alaska’s utilities and local leaders: the hydropower relicensing process is broken. With 40 percent of our nation’s non-federal hydropower licenses set to expire by 2035, including 12 projects in Alaska, we need to address the unwarranted delays and costly federal requirements that often bear little connection to a project’s direct impacts. Those burdens make it much harder to maintain and expand one of Alaska’s most reliable sources of renewable, baseload power. By ensuring mandatory licensing conditions are tied to a project’s direct adverse effects, this legislation will provide greater regulatory certainty, reduce unnecessary costs, and help keep electricity affordable and reliable for Alaskans. https://www.murkowski.senate.gov/press/release/murkowski-and-colleagues-lead-efforts-to-bolster-made-in-america-hydropower

There’s confusion about how the cap and Associated Entity language work in the Protect College Sports Act. Let me clear it up. The cap is a hard cap. Full stop. That loophole is closed. Once a school hits the cap, a player can still do NIL deals on the open market — if the deal is genuinely commercial and the school isn’t directing it. That’s the line. Some commissioners want more: bar any company doing business with a school from signing that school’s players. So a QB couldn’t sign with Nike because Nike has a separate contract with his university. That’s not protecting a cap. That’s blocking a kid from selling his own name. Every pro league works this way. If the team doesn’t direct it, the player earns it. What exactly is the objection? And we went further than anyone asked: players disclose all of their deals, and the university president AND the sponsor sign a letter certifying they stayed under the cap. Cheat, and you signed your name to it. Hard cap. Loophole closed. Players keep the right to earn what the school didn’t arrange. Those aren’t in tension — that’s the whole point.

Only eight command staff members in the history of the Middletown Township Police Department had ever graduated from the FBI National Academy. Last month, Lieutenant Aileen Parker, this week’s Hometown Hero, became the ninth. That is an extraordinary accomplishment, and one that reflects the officer, leader, and public servant she has proven herself to be throughout her career. As a former FBI Special Agent, I know the standard the FBI National Academy represents within law enforcement. Quantico is where proven officers and command leaders are challenged at the highest level — in judgment, discipline, communication, physical fitness, command presence, character, and the responsibility of leading the men and women who protect our families, neighborhoods, schools, and businesses. Lieutenant Parker earned her place there, and she brings that standard of excellence home to Middletown Township. But this achievement is not the sum of her career. It is a reflection of it. At MTPD, Lieutenant Parker has played a major role in the critically important, often unseen work that makes police departments strong: supervision, operations, training, accreditation, accountability, professional standards, officer development, and the daily leadership required to support officers and protect the community. She has continued to raise the standard at every level— completing the FBI-LEEDA Trilogy and graduating from Northwestern University’s School of Police Staff and Command, where she was selected by her peers to serve as class president and deliver the keynote address. Those achievements reflect what her colleagues already know: Lieutenant Parker leads with preparation, credibility, discipline, and earned respect. Strong communities need strong law enforcement. And strong law enforcement depends on leaders who keep learning, keep improving, keep supporting their officers, and keep bringing excellence back home. Lieutenant Parker is one of those leaders. Please join me in congratulating Lieutenant Aileen Parker on this outstanding achievement and thanking her for her service to Middletown Township. Here in PA-1, we are blessed to have some of the finest law enforcement officers anywhere in America. Let us come together to continue to thank them, support them, stand with them, and never take for granted the incredible men and women who put on the uniform, answer the call, and protect our families, neighborhoods, schools, businesses, and communities every single day.

When duplicative inspections and outdated federal requirements drive landlords out of affordable housing programs, families pay the price: fewer available homes, fewer choices, and longer waits for a place they can afford. Across our community, where limited supply and rising costs are already putting housing out of reach for too many families, these barriers were making an urgent challenge even worse. The Choice in Affordable Housing Act was one of the central initiatives I led as part our bipartisan Affordability Agenda. Signed into law earlier this month, this bill will modernize the Housing Choice Voucher program, strengthen landlord participation, and give more of our PA-1 families access to safe, affordable homes. This law is progress, but not the finish line. We will keep cutting barriers, expanding supply, and lowering housing costs across our community and nationwide.

Affordability is about whether families can put down roots, businesses can grow, and communities can thrive. My work with our local families, business owners, and community organizations helped shape the priorities I brought to the Problem Solvers Caucus, where colleagues from both side of the aisle came together to build our Bipartisan Affordability Agenda. Earlier this month, four bills from that agenda were signed into law—a major step forward, and momentum we are determined to build on. Thank you to the Cato Institute and Ryan Bourne for such a great conversation about what comes next, and how we continue turning affordability solutions shaped by the people and communities we serve into bipartisan law.

L000593.text: Trust in American institutions is at an all-time low, and it’s painfully obvious why.    Donald Trump wants corruption to feel so constant, so overwhelming, and so normal that Americans stop believing it can be defeated.    He wants us numb. He wants us exhausted. He wants us to give up.    But corruption only wins when we stop believing anything can be done about it.    I’m not backing down, and you shouldn’t either.

Is there anything the Trump Administration ISN’T corrupting and covering up? More than $16 million in taxpayer money wasted on a botched Reflecting Pool renovation. A White House employee using insider knowledge to make bets on prediction markets. A senior official pushed out after warning the White House about breaking the law. They don’t want you to know about any of it. That’s exactly why I’m laying it all out. https://youtu.be/0p_cR-aiwCI?si=SEO7EFEDRv7D52Xm

Donald Trump took America’s 250th birthday, handed it to a secretive operation run by his allies, and showered it with taxpayer money and private donations. He created a shadow company called Freedom 250 and diverted $75 million of the $100 million meant for the official, bipartisan America250 Commission. Then he placed Freedom 250 inside the National Park Foundation, an official charity that does not have to publicly disclose its donors. In other words: millions of dollars can pour into Trump’s operation, and the public does not get to know who is writing the checks. Now, after refusing to provide a full accounting of who paid or where the money went, Freedom 250 wants taxpayers to cough up another $10 million. Absolutely not. When I say this is the most corrupt administration in American history, I am not kidding.

Todd Blanche says the Trump Administration’s $1.8 billion payout fund is dead. But he STILL refuses to put that in writing. And while he insists the fund is gone, his Justice Department keeps finding other ways to hand seven-figure settlements to Trump allies. It just approved a massive taxpayer-funded payout to Paul Vaughn, an anti-abortion activist convicted of conspiring to block access to a health clinic—and later pardoned by Donald Trump. Call it a slush fund. Call it a settlement. Call it whatever you want. A different name does not change what is happening: The Trump Administration and the Justice Department are using taxpayer money to reward Trump’s allies. There is not a single person in this country asking for their tax dollars to be shoveled into the pockets of convicted Trump allies because the President believes they deserve a payday. And Todd Blanche wants the Senate to trust him with even more power? Absolutely not. He has shown us exactly how he would use the power of the Attorney General’s office. The Senate should not give him any more of it. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/29/us/politics/todd-blanche-weaponization-payouts.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share

The gravity of war demands more than improvisation. The current conflict in Iran was entered without the authorization our Constitution requires, and it has been conducted without the steady hand such a decision deserves. The peace that was promised has collapsed, and the fighting has resumed. Now the Administration argues that this renewed conflict resets the clock, granting another 60 days to wage war without a vote in Congress. That is not what the law provides. The power to commit this nation to war belongs to the people’s representatives, not to a single person reinterpreting the rules to suit his wishes. We must not treat war as something to be improvised. And we must not treat the law that governs it as something to be rewritten at will.

G000591.text: Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Richard Henry Lee was born in Virginia in 1732. At age 16, he sailed to England to continue his education. While he was studying in England, his parents died, leaving him an orphan. Returning to the colonies, Lee volunteered to raise a military company for the French and Indian War. In 1758, he was elected to the House of Burgesses. Seeking to serve his community, Lee applied to be a tax collector during the Stamp Act period. This led him to be censured and began his support for the cause for independence. While serving in the Second Continental Congress, he drafted what was known as the Lee Resolution that was used as guidance for the Declaration of Independence. He signed the Declaration in August of 1776.

I stopped by Branhilda Richardson Knowles Memorial Park in Deerfield Beach to pay respect to an important piece of our local history. I was proud to help secure funding for this park when I was a state legislator.   Born in the Bahamas, Branhilda Richardson Knowles came to Deerfield Beach in 1922 and served as a midwife for the African American community at a time when segregation denied many Black residents access to hospitals and other medical care.   The park that now bears her name also preserves a historic African American cemetery, where Black and Bahamian residents were buried during the Jim Crow era because they were prohibited from being laid to rest in the city cemetery.   Grateful to see how Deerfield Beach has worked to honor the people who helped build the community we know today.

On this day in history in 1945, the USS Indianapolis is sunk by a Japanese submarine after carrying the atomic bomb across the Pacific Ocean. The cruiser was en route to the Philippines when one torpedo took the bow of the ship off followed by a second that hit the midsection and blew the ship nearly in two. The USS Indianapolis sunk in 12 minutes, with 300 of its almost 1,200 person crew going down with it. The remaining 890 fought to survive for four days before the Navy learned of the catastrophic event. During this time, the crew faced saltwater poisoning, dehydration, and shark attacks. By the time they were rescued, there were only 316 survivors, making it the greatest loss at sea from a single ship in the history of the US Navy, as well as the “worst shark attack in history.”

On this day in history in 1958, @NASA is established as President Eisenhower signs into law the National Aeronautics and Space Act. ROAD TO 250: Long Island & Queens Legacies Target Rock in Lloyd Harbor is more than a scenic landmark—it is a reminder of Long Island’s place in our nation’s history. The wildlife refuge takes its name from a 14-foot-tall glacial boulder standing just offshore in Huntington Bay. For generations, the rock served as a navigation marker for mariners and was reportedly used for cannon and target practice during both the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. During the American Revolution, the British established "East Fort" nearby to help defend the harbor, and Lloyd Neck became home to Loyalists displaced by the conflict. As America approaches its 250th anniversary, places like Target Rock help tell the story of how the Revolutionary War shaped communities here on Long Island and across the nation.

We discussed the tremendous potential of the Kodiak Spaceport Complex, one of the nation's critical commercial launch sites, as well as Poker Flat Research Range outside of Fairbanks, the world's only university-owned rocket range and a cornerstone of atmospheric and space research.   As investment in aerospace continues to grow, we have an incredible opportunity to prepare Alaska's students, engineers and technicians for high-paying careers right here at home. By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: Face à la situation migratoire à Ceuta, j’ai été en contact avec le Président du gouvernement espagnol pour marquer notre solidarité et proposer toute aide nécessaire, y compris via Frontex. Je salue la coopération en cours avec le Maroc, qui a déjà permis aujourd’hui plus de 40 000 retours de Ceuta vers le Maroc. Les ministres de l’Intérieur sont en contact pour assurer un suivi étroit de la situation. Ceuta ne bénéficie pas de la libre circulation vers le reste de l’espace Schengen. J’ai toutefois demandé dès hier au Ministre de l’Intérieur de renforcer les contrôles à notre frontière avec l’Espagne si cela devait être nécessaire : 4 unités de forces mobiles, des avions et des drones sont déployés. Ces mesures viennent renforcer les dispositions que nous avons prises depuis 2020 pour mieux protéger notre frontière avec l’Espagne en étroite coordination, avec des brigades communes et une action conjointe de lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. Ces mesures viennent compléter les instruments européens adoptés pour assurer les retours et appliquer le pacte asile et migrations, avec 25% de chute des flux irréguliers vers l’Union européenne l’an dernier et une baisse poursuivie sur les routes migratoires atlantique et de Méditerranée occidentale en 2026. Solidarité et responsabilité avec nos partenaires européens pour faire appliquer nos règles de fermeté en matière de retours et de protection des frontières extérieures de l’Union. Je redis ici notre solidarité à l’Espagne, son gouvernement et son peuple.
